why: the cross-thread / ISR wake source, created on the NODE so it lands in the owning executor's arena (static entity storage: the executor's entity table is an arena sized at compile time (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`) with no allocator behind it, and a `HandleId` is an index into it. Registration is one-way -- no slot is ever reclaimed and no handle is ever invalidated.). rclcpp constructs an `rclcpp::GuardCondition` free-standing from a `Context` and a caller adds it to a wait set; with no wait set (rclcpp's wait-set protocol; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.) the executor has to own it, so creation has to go through something that knows the executor. The scenario is the one an RTOS actually has: an ISR or a driver task has data and must release a `spin_once` blocked in `drive_io` before its poll timeout expires. phase-417 W4.e made this shape the one all three languages use -- C took `rclc_node_create_guard_condition` and Rust took `Node::create_guard_condition`, so this row stopped being C++'s own arrangement and became the decision. The free-standing constructor from a `Context` stays refused; that argument is made in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.
